source_text: Inde gratiam ostendit esse laudabilem, si ei per omnia conveniret, quod dixit: Iudicium ex uno in condemnationem, gratia autem ex multis delictis in iustificationem [n174] . Qua tu ergo licentia gratiam Christi ea laudatione fraudabis, qua illam Apostolus voluit praedicari; ut deicias titulum dignitatis, per quem solum honorem eius vas electionis voluit agnosci?
pass_a_gloss: From there he showed grace to be praiseworthy, if that agreed with it through all things which he said: Judgment from one into condemnation, but grace from many offenses into justification. With what license therefore will you defraud the grace of Christ of that praise by which the Apostle wanted it to be preached; so that you throw down the title of dignity, through which alone the vessel of election wanted its honor to be recognized?

lemmas.lexica: LS delictum; Blaise Rom 5 delictum vs donum
LS iustificatio; Blaise forensic making-just, not later system
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'
LS electio=choice; Blaise not later predestination 'election' unless forced

pass_b_english: He thus showed grace to be praiseworthy if what he said applied to it fully: ‘The judgment was from one to condemnation, but grace is from many offenses to justification’ (Romans 5:16) (Acts 9:15). By what license, then, will you rob Christ’s grace of the praise with which the apostle wished it proclaimed? Will you cast down the title of dignity through which alone the chosen vessel wished its honor to be recognized (allusion to Acts 9:15)?

choices.why: Paul's delictum of the one man; an act, not a nature.
Paul's iustificatio vitae; keep forensic making-just, not a later systematic slogan as default.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

variants.reading: In this quotation the Latin leaves the noun after “one” unstated. The surrounding argument discusses what must be supplied; no noun has been silently inserted into the quotation.
